Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Hairdresser
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Mai was nineteen and working as a hairdresser at a salon in a strip mall when the accident happened. She had been driving home after a long shift, her mind still half on the client who had wanted a complicated balayage, when she saw the boy—maybe seven years old—break away from his mother on the sidewalk and sprint straight into the crosswalk without looking. Mai slammed the brakes, but the car hit him. The sound of the impact was a dull, heavy thud that seemed to come from inside her own chest, and then the screaming started—the mother’s scream, the boy’s thin wail, the screech of the tires on the asphalt still ringing in her ears. She got out of the car and saw him lying on the ground, his leg bent at an angle that made her stomach turn. She dialed 911 with shaking hands, and while she waited, she kept saying “I’m sorry” over and over, but the words felt useless. The boy survived, but the doctors said he would need multiple surgeries and might never walk normally again. Mai was never charged—the family’s lawyer made it clear the boy had run out without warning—but that did not matter to her.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of the accident came back to her not as a story she could tell but as a series of pictures that appeared without warning: the boy’s startled face just before impact, the unnatural angle of his leg, the mother’s hands flying up to her mouth. Loud noises of any kind could set it off—a car horn in traffic, a door slamming in the salon—and she would feel her heart race, her palms go slick with sweat, and for a moment she would be right back on that street corner. Sometimes, when the images came, she would feel nothing at all. She would recall the whole scene with a strange, hollow numbness, as if it had happened to someone else, as if she were watching a movie. And then, just as suddenly, the grief would hit her—a raw, wordless sorrow that made her want to curl up on the floor and cry for that boy and his mother and for herself, for the person she used to be before she had done this.

Mai stopped driving completely. She asked her boyfriend to drive her to work, or she took the bus, even if it meant an extra forty minutes each way. She could not bear the thought of being behind the wheel again, and she could barely tolerate being a passenger, flinching every time the car approached an intersection. She also began to avoid the anniversary of the accident. When the date came close, she told her boss she needed a personal day and stayed in her apartment with the curtains drawn, refusing to look at the calendar.

At the salon, Mai became excessively compliant. When a client complained about the cut, she apologized and offered a free redo even when the cut was fine. When her coworker asked her to stay late, she said yes even though she was exhausted. She had come to believe that she could not trust herself—if her own body could cause such harm without her intending it, then she had no right to assert herself, to say no. She had failed to protect that boy, so she would try to protect everyone else now by never causing any friction, never being a problem. This fawn response had started to drain her. She would go home and lie on the couch, unable to relax even in her own bedroom, because she was always scanning for threats. In the salon, she had memorized the location of every exit the first day she returned to work. In a restaurant with her boyfriend, she would sit facing the door, her eyes darting to the back hallway every few minutes. He had started to ask why she seemed so on edge, and she did not know how to explain that her body had become a liability, that she no longer trusted herself to be safe around others.

What finally brought Mai to seek help was a panic attack that hit her in the middle of a haircut. A client had brought her toddler, and the child slipped off the chair and let out a sharp cry. Mai heard it and froze, the sound dissolving into the memory of the boy’s wail. She dropped her scissors and had to run to the back room, her hands shaking, her chest tight. The salon manager asked if she was okay, and Mai said yes, but she knew she was not. She made an appointment with a therapist that afternoon. What she was most afraid of, she told herself, was that she would never feel normal again—that she would always be this version of herself, jumpy, compliant, grieving. But what she hoped for, in a small and barely acknowledged corner of her mind, was that someone could help her understand why she could not let the accident go, even though everyone else had told her it was not her fault.

missing_explanations: The vignette does not depict Mai's belief that she cannot rely on other people. She relies on her boyfriend for rides and seeks help from a therapist, which suggests some reliance, but the specific negative appraisal is absent.
